avoid.reason: Watch for touts and inflated tea/souvenir prices around Tunxi Old Street and cable-car queue jumping in peak season.

hood_desc: A pedestrian Ming-and-Qing-dynasty street of black-tile, white-wall shophouses selling Huizhou ink, tea, and carved inkstones — the city's most walkable, central base.

Tangkou is the gateway town at Mount Huangshan's south gate, about 65 km north of Tunxi, lined with hotels, guesthouses and restaurants around the transfer hub for the mountain shuttle buses. It suits hikers who want an early start on the mountain, though it is a functional transit town with little to see and an hour from Tunxi's old streets.
Twin UNESCO-listed Huizhou villages of whitewashed courtyard homes reflected in ox-shaped ponds, a short bus ride from Tunxi.

Liyang is an old quarter on the south bank of the river facing Tunxi Old Street, where the restored Liyang In Lane mixes Huizhou-style houses with glass-fronted shops, inns and cafes. It suits visitors who want a characterful base a short walk over the bridge from Old Street, though much of the lane is rebuilt in modern style and choice inside it is small.

landmarks: Huangshan (Yellow Mountain) Scenic Area
China's most painted mountain, a UNESCO landscape of granite spires, gnarled pines and swirling seas of cloud that inspired centuries of poets.
Hongcun Ancient Village
A UNESCO-listed Ming-era water village whose moon pond and whitewashed Huizhou mansions starred in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon.
Xidi Ancient Village
Hongcun's UNESCO twin, an exquisitely preserved merchant village of carved stone archways, black-tiled roofs and nearly a thousand years of Huizhou heritage.
West Sea Grand Canyon (Xihai Great Canyon)
Yellow Mountain's most thrilling sector, where plank paths and stairways cling to sheer granite walls above a fantasy landscape of mist-wrapped pinnacles.
Greeting-Guests Pine (Yingkesong)
An 800-year-old pine extending a welcoming bough beside Jade Screen Peak, so iconic it appears in the Great Hall of the People.
Tunxi Old Street (Tunxi Laojie)
A flagstone street of Ming and Qing storefronts in Huangshan city, perfect for browsing ink stones, tea and street snacks beneath red lanterns.
Bright Summit (Guangming Peak)
Yellow Mountain's second-highest point and its finest sunrise stage, where crowds gather at dawn to watch clouds ignite over an ocean of peaks.
Tangyue Memorial Archways
Seven monumental stone arches marching across the fields near Shexian, Ming and Qing tributes to the loyalty and virtue of the Bao family.
Huizhou Ancient City (Shexian)
One of China's four great ancient cities, a walled county seat of gate towers, the grand Xuguo Stone Archway and living Huizhou traditions.
Chengkan Village
A feng-shui masterpiece village laid out on the bagua pattern, its Baolun Hall ranking among the finest Ming ancestral buildings in southern China.

train.note: Huangshan has no international trains. Huangshan North, open since 2015, is the high-speed station with services to Hangzhou in about 1.5 hours plus Shanghai, Nanjing, Nanchang, Qingdao, Fuzhou, Guangzhou and Beijing; the older Huangshan station in Tunxi handles conventional trains, including an overnight service from Shanghai via Suzhou and Nanjing that takes about 11 hours and arrives around 07:00, leaving you a full day on the mountain. Book on 12306 with your passport, and remember that both stations are in Huangshan City (Tunxi), an hour short of the mountain itself.

bus.note: No international coaches serve Huangshan. Direct buses run from Shanghai and Hangzhou to the main Huangshan (Tunxi) bus station, and from there frequent services continue to Tangkou at the foot of the mountain in about an hour, with some long-distance coaches running through to Tangkou directly. Return coaches from the mountain generally leave in the early to mid afternoon, so do not leave the descent too late. Tickets are sold at the terminal counters.

ferry.note: There are no passenger ferry services to or from Huangshan; it is an inland city in the hills of southern Anhui. The only boats in the area are sightseeing cruises on Taiping Lake, on the northern side of the mountain, which are sold as an excursion rather than as transport.

half.name: Wuyuan Ancient Villages
half.blurb: A cluster of Hui-style villages with white-walled courtyard houses, said to be among the best-preserved in China, roughly two hours from Huangshan by road.

half.name: Mount Qiyun (Qiyunshan)
half.blurb: A Taoist mountain in Xiuning County dotted with cliffside temples, grottoes, and carved inscriptions, reached in under two hours from central Huangshan.

half.name: Jingdezhen
half.blurb: China's historic porcelain-making city, with kiln museums and working ceramic workshops, roughly two hours away by train.

half.name: Qimen
half.blurb: A tea-growing county southwest of Huangshan known for Keemun black tea plantations and processing workshops.

half.name: Shexian (Huizhou Ancient City)
half.blurb: Former Huizhou prefectural seat with Ming and Qing gates, lanes, wells and memorial archways.

full.name: Mount Huangshan (Huangshan Scenic Area)
full.blurb: UNESCO-listed granite range of pine-clad peaks and cloud seas, climbed by stone steps or cable car from Tangkou's south gate.

notes.walk: Tunxi's Old Street and riverside areas are very walkable; the mountain itself demands serious hiking or cable cars, and the ancient villages are best explored on foot along cobblestone lanes
notes.card: Credit cards are rarely accepted outside international hotels; WeChat Pay and Alipay are used for almost everything — set up mobile payment before arrival and carry some cash as backup
notes.safety: Very safe for solo travelers, including women; petty crime is rare. Low — occasional overcharging by unlicensed taxis or tour touts near the mountain entrance is the main annoyance.
notes.religion: Buddhism and Taoism (mixed folk practice); majority nonreligious / ancestor veneration; small Christian minority
notes.langs: Mandarin Chinese; Huizhou (Hui) dialect; limited English in tourist areas
notes.net: Good 4G/5G coverage in Tunxi and along main roads; patchy on remote mountain trails. Free wifi in most hotels and cafes, though speeds vary. ~$3-5 per GB on a prepaid tourist SIM. The Great Firewall blocks Google, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook — install a VPN before arrival. Buy a SIM or eSIM at Shanghai/Hangzhou airport before onward travel; Tunxi Airport's counter has limited stock.
notes.transit: City buses (Huangshan Bus Group) plus scenic-area shuttle buses
notes.transport: Huangshan Tunxi International Airport (TXN), ~7 km from Tunxi, with flights to Shanghai, Beijing, Guangzhou, and other major Chinese cities. Huangshan North railway station sits on the Hefei–Fuzhou and Shanghai–Kunming high-speed lines — about 3 hrs from Shanghai, 1.5 hrs from Hangzhou. Long-distance buses connect Huangshan to Hangzhou, Shanghai, and Nanjing; local buses run from Tunxi to Tangkou (mountain base) and the ancient villages. None — Huangshan is inland with no scheduled passenger ferry service. Self-driving or a hired car is common for reaching Hongcun, Xidi, and Shexian; roads are good but mountain-area driving and parking get congested in peak season.
